additional_requirements: The binge eating and inappropriate compensatory behaviors both occur, on average, at least once a week for 3 months

S046.name: Body_Image_Weight_Shape_Disturbance
S046.description: Undue influence of body weight or shape on self-evaluation.

subtypes.Distorted Body Image: Perceiving one's body as much fatter than it actually is or perceiving specific parts as excessively large when looking in the mirror.
subtypes.Self-Worth Dependent on Weight: Judging whether one is a good or successful person solely based on weight or body shape.

S048.name: Compensatory_Behavior_Purging
S048.description: Recurrent inappropriate compensatory behaviors involving the expulsion of food or fluids to prevent weight gain.

subtypes.Self-Induced Vomiting: Intentionally inducing vomiting to remove ingested food.
subtypes.Misuse of Medications: Repetitively misusing laxatives, diuretics, or enemas for the purpose of weight control.

S049.name: Eating_Large_Amount
S049.description: Eating, in a discrete period of time, an amount of food that is definitely larger than what most individuals would eat in a similar period of time under similar circumstances.
examples: Eating more than 3-4 times the amount of a typical meal within 2 hours.
Continuously eating large amounts of high-calorie snacks in addition to main meals.
Eating enough to empty a significant portion of the refrigerator or pantry at once.
Eating clearly more food than others during the same period of time.

S050.name: Loss_of_Control
S050.description: A sense of lack of control over eating during the episode (e.g., a feeling that one cannot stop eating or control what or how much one is eating).
examples: A feeling that once I start eating, I cannot stop even if I want to.
Thinking 'I shouldn't eat any more' but mechanically continuing to eat.
A feeling of helplessness that I cannot decide for myself how much to eat.
Eating as if my body is being controlled by someone else.

symptom.disease_info: Bulimia nervosa is an eating disorder characterized by recurrent episodes of binge eating followed by inappropriate compensatory behaviors such as self‑induced vomiting, laxative misuse, fasting, or excessive exercise, typically driven by an overvaluation of weight and shape. Individuals usually maintain a body weight in or near the normal range, which helps distinguish it from classic anorexia nervosa, though there can be overlap. The course is often fluctuating, with periods of more and less intense symptoms, and it is frequently associated with shame, secrecy, and significant psychosocial distress. It is distinguished from binge‑eating disorder by the presence of regular compensatory behaviors and from normal dieting or overeating by the sense of loss of control and the central role of body image in self‑evaluation.

patient.stressor: About a year before presentation, Jennifer’s husband was diagnosed with congestive heart failure, and she took on most of his caregiving while continuing her part‑time retail job and community activities. At the same time, her own doctor began emphasizing weight loss and stricter dietary control to help her blood pressure and joint pain, and comments about her BMI at routine visits made her increasingly self‑conscious given her long‑standing role as the church baker and "treat" person at gatherings. Over the ensuing seven months, she quietly shifted from enjoying her baked goods in moderation to eating large amounts alone after stressful days of caregiving and then going to great lengths afterward to "undo" what she had eaten, all while keeping up a competent, sociable front at work and in her clubs. She finally agreed to see a mental health clinician after her primary care physician noticed unexplained fluctuations in her electrolytes and dental wear at a check‑up, gently raised concerns about her eating patterns, and suggested that the distress she described about her behavior wasn’t "just stress" and might benefit from specialized help.
patient.chief_complaint: I keep trying to get rid of what I eat after I overdo it, and I feel like I can’t stop doing it on my own.

patient.stressor: Bobby’s symptoms began to escalate during his first semester at a local community college, when the combination of a heavier course load, commuting, and his tendency to procrastinate led to missed assignments and a sharp drop in grades. Away from the familiar structure of high school clubs and family dinners, he started eating irregularly, then discovered that late‑night snacking while coding or watching videos temporarily eased his anxiety about falling behind, which gradually turned into episodes of consuming far more than he intended. Over roughly seven months, these episodes became more frequent around exam periods, and he started using drastic measures afterward in an attempt to "reset" and control his weight, which he felt was creeping up because of all the fast food and dorm snacks. He presented to the college counseling center after nearly failing a key class, feeling frightened by how often he was eating far more than he planned to and what he was doing afterward to compensate, especially when a professor suggested he might need to take a leave if his concentration and attendance didn’t improve.
patient.chief_complaint: When I start eating, especially at night, I feel like I can’t stop or control how much I’m eating anymore.

patient.stressor: Dianne was promoted to supervise a larger construction crew on a high‑profile historic renovation about eight months ago, a role that came with tighter deadlines, more visibility, and frequent interactions with architects and city officials. As one of the few women on‑site, she became increasingly aware of comments about her appearance and fitness from coworkers and joking remarks about "keeping up" physically, which intersected with social media images of lean, athletic women in the trades that she followed for inspiration. Over the next seven months, she responded by trying to rigidly control her eating during the day, but work stress, long hours, and post‑game barbecues with her softball league led to repeated evenings where she felt she had "blown it" and then went to extremes afterward to try to compensate and keep her weight from changing. She sought psychiatric care after her spouse, worried by her growing preoccupation with her size, pointed out how much her mood and self‑esteem now seemed to hinge on the scale and how "good" or "bad" she thought her body looked in work gear, prompting Dianne to admit that her focus on her weight and shape had begun to overshadow her enjoyment of both work and home life.
patient.chief_complaint: My whole sense of worth feels tied up in what I weigh and how my body looks, and it’s taking over my life.
